conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically in the past seven days, since having your baby.  

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team; the goal is to give you a safe, non-judgmental space to talk about the very real ups and downs of new motherhood. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words—no right or wrong answers.  

Ready to begin?  

**Question 1:** Over the last week, how much have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not much… I can’t remember the last time I really laughed. I might smile if someone shows me a cute video of the baby, but it feels forced, like I’m just doing it to be polite. Most of the time I’m too tired or worried to find anything funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very often… I’ll give a little chuckle if my husband tries to joke, but it’s like the happiness doesn’t reach me. I hear myself make the sound, yet inside I still feel flat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to—like I keep telling myself I’ll feel better if I get out for a walk or meet a friend for coffee—but when the time comes, it just feels… blah. I used to get excited about little plans, even just a new show to binge, but lately it’s like I’m going through the motions. I’ll think “this should be fun,” yet I barely feel that spark anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s something I’m doing wrong—maybe I’m not feeding her right, or I missed some cue. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk and I sat on the nursery floor crying because “that was her food and I wasted it.” My head tells me it was just an accident, but inside I’m sure it proves I’m failing her somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day… like my heart races the moment she makes a weird grunt or if the monitor flickers. I’ll stand over her crib watching her breathe, convinced something’s wrong even though she’s fine. And when everything’s quiet, I’m still tense—waiting for something bad to happen. I know it doesn’t make sense, but I can’t shake the feeling.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it hits me out of nowhere. I’ll be folding her tiny onesies and suddenly my chest gets tight, my hands shake, and I feel like I can’t catch my breath. There’s no real danger, but for a few minutes I’m sure something awful is about to happen. It passes if I pace or do the breathing app on my phone, but those waves of panic show up almost every day.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. Between the feedings, the laundry pile, trying to sleep in tiny windows… it feels like I’m drowning in stuff that never gets finished. I’ll start one chore, hear her cry, drop everything, and by evening nothing’s done and I’m just exhausted. Sometimes I sit on the couch staring at the mess, thinking, “I can’t keep up,” but I still manage to get the basics done somehow.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s been rough at night. Even when she’s asleep, my mind keeps spinning—Did I burp her enough? Is she breathing? Am I doing any of this right? I’ll lie there for an hour or two, totally worn out but wide awake. Sometimes I drift off, then jolt up for no reason and can’t settle again. I’m lucky if I get three or four broken hours before she needs me.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… it’s like a gray cloud that just sticks around. I’ll be feeding her and tears start rolling—no real reason, just this heavy sadness sitting on my chest. Most afternoons I end up staring out the window feeling empty, wondering if I’ll ever feel like myself again.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

It happens a few times a week. Yesterday I put her in the car seat, couldn’t get the buckle to click right away, and suddenly I was sobbing in the garage. It’s never about just the buckle—it’s everything piling up—and the tears come before I can stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I’m exhausted and overwhelmed, but I’d never want to leave her or let anything happen to me. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

You've shared how, since your baby arrived, joy feels out of reach: laughter is hollow, plans feel flat, and a gray cloud of sadness lingers. You blame yourself when small things go wrong, describe daily waves of worry and sudden panic, and find nights filled with anxious thoughts that steal your already limited sleep. Despite these heavy feelings, you remain devoted to your daughter and want to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, forced laughter without felt joy, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes marked loss of anticipatory pleasure—plans feel "blah," "no spark," consistent with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame over minor incidents, aligning with "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, pervasive, irrational worries (monitor flickers, baby grunts) and persistent dread, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes occurring almost daily with physical symptoms (tight chest, shaking, breathlessness) and catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>She describes frequent, daily overwhelm but still managing basics, aligning with "sometimes not coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia driven by anxious, intrusive thoughts and repeated awakenings, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, tearful sadness with no clear trigger and a sense of emptiness, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes tearful episodes a few times a week triggered by everyday stressors, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total of 24 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. Key items align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: persistent low mood (<quote>gray cloud that just sticks around</quote>), markedly diminished interest (<quote>no spark</quote>), excessive inappropriate guilt (<quote>convinced I'm failing her</quote>), fatigue, insomnia, and recurrent tearfulness. High scores on questions 4 and 5 also flag prominent <med>postpartum anxiety</med> with daily panic symptoms. Item 10 is negative, so no current self-harm alert. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>primary care physician</med> to review results and discuss treatment options including <med>evidence-based therapy</med> and/or medication
2. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor symptom trend
3. Begin practical support: enlist family or friends for night shifts or household tasks so you can secure 3-4 hour blocks of sleep
4. Incorporate 5-10 minutes of gentle movement or outdoor light daily to help regulate mood and anxiety
5. Keep crisis numbers handy (e.g., Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773) and call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department if you ever experience thoughts of self-harm
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant approx. ≤3 mo)  
Date: [today]  
Screener: Licensed MHP  

A. Positive findings (EPDS-relevant items)  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (Q1, 2, 8, 9)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Marked anxiety: racing heart, intrusive “what-if” thoughts, nightly checking respirations (Q4)  
- Panic-equivalent episodes (tight chest, dyspnea, tremor) without clear trigger, ≥1× daily (Q5)  
- Subjective “drowning” feeling, difficulty completing tasks (Q6)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia directly linked to ruminating worries (Q7)  

B. Pattern summary  
Symptoms cluster around depressive (mood, pleasure loss, guilt) and anxiety (free-floating worry, panic) domains; onset post-delivery; functional impact moderate (household tasks, social withdrawal, daytime fatigue). No psychotic content.  

C. Safety  
Self-harm ideation: Denied (Q10); no plan or intent documented. No current safety concern but will continue to monitor.  

D. Screening conclusion  
Presentation exceeds threshold for probable clinically significant postpartum depression with prominent anxiety features; recommend formal assessment (DSM-5-TR criteria) and discussion of treatment options with OB/MH provider.
